Where it began

Ricky Ponting arrived on 19 December 1974 in Launceston, in the north of Tasmania, and was the eldest of three. Sport was in the family. His father Graeme was a good club cricketer, his mother Lorraine was a state champion at vigoro, and his uncle, Greg Campbell, was a Test cricketer. It was his father and uncle who first put a bat in his hands.

At 11 he was playing for the Mowbray Under-13s, and before long he was making hundreds by the handful in junior cricket. He also loved Australian football, but a badly broken arm at 13 settled that question. After leaving school he worked as a groundsman, until a two-week stay at the Australian Cricket Academy in Adelaide turned into two years. In November 1992, at 17, he became the youngest man to play Sheffield Shield cricket for Tasmania.

The player

He made 96 in his first Test, at Perth in December 1995 against Sri Lanka, and his first Test hundred came in an Ashes Test in England in 1997. From there he grew into one of the great run-makers. In 168 Tests between 1995 and 2012 he scored 13,378 runs at 51.85, with 41 hundreds and 62 fifties, and a highest score of 257. He also held 196 catches, many of them at slip.

As captain he led Australia in 77 Tests and won 48 of them. He led Australia to victory at the World Cups of 2003 and 2007 and the Champions Trophies of 2006 and 2009, having already been part of the side that won the World Cup in 1999.

What made him special

He was a natural stroke player who loved to take the game to the bowlers, and a superb slip fielder. Rod Marsh, who coached him at the Academy, thought he was the best 17-year-old batter he had seen. He was the first man to be part of 100 Test wins.

Spin on Indian pitches was the one puzzle that took him time. On the 2001 tour Harbhajan Singh got him out every time he batted, which must have made for some long evenings of thinking.

Away from the middle

He was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, was made an Officer of the Order of Australia, and entered the ICC Hall of Fame in July 2018. After leaving Test cricket in November 2012, with his 168th Test equalling Steve Waugh's Australian record, he went on to coach and commentate, and in February 2019 he became an assistant coach of the Australian men's side. Away from cricket, his football team was the North Melbourne Kangaroos.

And finally

As a boy he helped work the scoreboard at Shield matches in Launceston, just to be near the international players. It was a fine way to learn the game, and in time he put plenty of numbers up on scoreboards of his own.
